claims.text: At 500–700°C, the wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is primarily governed by formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer forms in situ during high-temperature wear.
The oxide layer stabilizes the coating microstructure.
The oxide layer reduces friction during wear.
Pre-oxidation annealing can produce a controlled, uniform oxide layer on the FeNiCrCoCu coating before wear testing.
Elevated-temperature oxidation of FeNiCrCoCu forms a protective oxide barrier.
The oxide barrier reduces direct metal-to-metal contact during wear.
The oxide barrier lowers the friction coefficient.
The oxide barrier prevents further oxidation.
The oxide barrier mitigates subsurface damage and microstructural degradation.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have lower wear rates than as-deposited coatings tested under identical high-temperature conditions.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have lower friction than as-deposited coatings tested under identical high-temperature conditions.
Pre-oxidized coatings will exhibit smoother wear tracks because of reduced friction.
A stable, adherent oxide layer will remain observable on pre-oxidized coatings after high-temperature wear.
The proposed oxide-controlled wear mechanism applies from approximately 500°C to 700°C under loads typical of industrial protective coatings.
At room temperature or under very low load, mechanisms other than oxide-layer protection may dominate wear.
Phase transformations or Cu-rich segregation may concurrently influence wear behavior.

contradictions.description: The governing layer is described as forming in situ during wear, whereas the intervention introduces an oxide layer before wear. The comparison therefore does not isolate whether in situ oxide formation, rather than merely the presence or effects of a preformed layer or annealing, governs wear.

The predicted causal relation requires an observed oxide layer to reduce wear and friction, but the falsification rule requires both absence of performance improvement and absence of the oxide layer. An intact oxide layer with no wear or friction benefit would directly challenge the mechanism yet would not satisfy the stated falsification rule; conversely, failure to form the layer is primarily an intervention failure.
